Nine places to go deeper than this lesson, or to check a citation yourself before it goes
into a real Lakeshore document. All nine were checked and loading at the time this page was
written.

- **[21 CFR Part 7, Subpart A, Section 7.3, Cornell Legal Information Institute](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/21/7.3)**
  — the full definitions section this lesson quotes from: recall, market withdrawal, stock
  recovery, and the Class I/II/III recall classification, all in one place. Worth reading in
  full once to see how tightly FDA defines each term.

- **[21 CFR Part 7, Subpart C, Section 7.41, eCFR](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/chapter-I/subchapter-A/part-7/subpart-C/section-7.41)**
  — the six-factor health hazard evaluation this lesson walks against Lakeshore's plasma lot.
  eCFR's "current as of" banner is useful for confirming you're reading the in-force version,
  not an amended-out one.

- **[FDA, "CDER GCP Inspections and Outcomes" (PDF)](https://www.fda.gov/media/164382/download)**
  — the same presentation module 1 used for the NAI/VAI/OAI slide, reused here for its
  Warning Letter slide (17). **Read it with the same scope caveat**: this is a presentation
  about Good Clinical Practice (GCP) inspections of clinical drug trials, not about CGMP
  inspections of a manufacturing or blood-collection facility. Only the Warning Letter's
  general character — public, redacted, informal and advisory — transfers; the clinical-trial
  content around it does not.

- **[FDA, Recalls, Market Withdrawals, & Safety Alerts](https://www.fda.gov/safety/recalls-market-withdrawals-safety-alerts)**
  — FDA's own public landing page for actual, real recall notices across every product type
  it regulates. Useful for seeing what a real recall classification and public notice actually
  look like in practice, without treating any single listed recall as a stand-in for
  Lakeshore's fictional scenario.

- **[Inspection Readiness: How to Respond to FDA 483s and Avoid Warning
  Letters](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xnadb4-ANiQ)** (NSF, from oEmbed `author_name`) — the
  video embedded in this lesson. An industry training webinar on answering a 483 so it does not
  escalate; it covers the Warning Letter thread only, is not blood-specific, and says nothing
  authoritative about Part 7 recalls. Verified embeddable via YouTube oEmbed on 2026-11-11
  (HTTP 200).

- **[FDA, Warning Letters](https://www.fda.gov/inspections-compliance-enforcement-and-criminal-investigations/compliance-actions-and-activities/warning-letters)**
  — FDA's own landing page for issued Warning Letters. Read it to see the instrument as FDA
  presents it publicly; do not treat any listed letter as a stand-in for Lakeshore's fictional
  situation. Verified loading via `curl` on 2026-11-11 (HTTP 200).

- **[FDA, Regulatory Procedures Manual](https://www.fda.gov/inspections-compliance-enforcement-and-criminal-investigations/compliance-manuals/regulatory-procedures-manual)**
  — FDA's internal-procedures manual for its own staff, published publicly; its chapters cover
  how the agency handles advisory actions and recalls. Useful when you want FDA's own process
  rather than a law firm's summary. Verified loading via `curl` on 2026-11-11 (HTTP 200).

- **[FDA guidance: Initiation of Voluntary Recalls Under 21 CFR Part 7, Subpart C](https://www.fda.gov/regulatory-information/search-fda-guidance-documents/initiation-voluntary-recalls-under-21-cfr-part-7-subpart-c)**
  — FDA's own (non-binding) guidance on being ready to start a voluntary recall and working with
  FDA through one. This is where to go for how firms are expected to prepare, beyond what the
  regulation text itself says. Verified loading via `curl` on 2026-11-11 (HTTP 200).

- **[21 CFR 7.46, Cornell LII](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/21/7.46)** — the
  firm-initiated recall section with the nine-item list and FDA's classification sentence. Check
  here for current text. Verified loading via `curl` on 2026-11-11 (HTTP 200).
